themes.name: CNN Architecture Benchmarking on Fashion-MNIST
themes.description: A large body of work systematically evaluates CNN architectures of varying depth and complexity on Fashion-MNIST, establishing performance baselines. Studies range from simple two-block CNNs achieving ~88–90% accuracy to optimized residual networks reaching 96%+. These provide important context for interpreting results from a small CNN.

themes.name: Effect of Data Augmentation on CNN Generalization
themes.description: Several studies directly measure how standard geometric augmentations (flips, rotations, translations, shifts) affect CNN classification accuracy and overfitting. The consistent finding is that augmentation improves generalization, particularly for small datasets or short training runs, though the magnitude varies by architecture and domain.

themes.name: Advanced and Adaptive Augmentation Strategies
themes.description: A distinct research thread moves beyond basic geometric transforms toward class-conditional, policy-optimized, or generative augmentation methods. These approaches (WeMix, MFG Augment, LMix, class-adaptive policies, VAEs) seek to correct distribution shift introduced by augmentation or adapt transforms per class, and consistently outperform naive augmentation on standard benchmarks.

themes.name: Hyperparameter and Regularization Tuning on Fashion-MNIST
themes.description: Multiple studies treat Fashion-MNIST as a testbed for examining the interaction between hyperparameters (filter size, batch size, dropout rate, learning rate, normalization placement) and model accuracy. These papers highlight that architecture choices and regularization can dominate augmentation effects, complicating isolated analysis.

themes.name: Transfer Learning and Lightweight CNNs
themes.description: A pragmatic thread addresses deployment constraints by building efficient lightweight CNNs or fine-tuning pre-trained models, often combining augmentation with transfer learning. These studies show that augmentation's benefit is architecture- and data-scale-dependent, and diminishes when pre-trained representations are available.

themes.name: Quantum and Hybrid CNN Architectures
themes.description: An emerging niche applies quantum computing concepts to CNN design on Fashion-MNIST, replacing classical convolutional filters with quantum circuits. While parameter-efficient, these approaches currently underperform classical CNNs on complex tasks and remain limited by hardware constraints.

overview.summary:
The use of convolutional neural networks (CNNs) for image classification on Fashion-MNIST is a well-established benchmark, with dozens of studies reporting accuracies ranging from roughly 88% for simple architectures up to ~99.65% for heavily optimized models. Data augmentation — including basic geometric transforms like flips, rotations, and translations — is widely recognized as a practical regularization tool that reduces overfitting and improves generalization, especially in low-data or short-training regimes.

Despite the abundance of Fashion-MNIST studies, clean controlled comparisons isolating the effect of basic augmentation on a small CNN are surprisingly rare: most papers either apply augmentation as one component in a larger optimization pipeline, or omit it entirely. The field has matured toward increasingly complex architectures and augmentation strategies (Mixup, CutOut, AutoAugment), which makes the proposed study's focused, reproducible, seed-controlled design a useful empirical baseline contribution.
open_problems: Isolating the contribution of basic augmentation from other simultaneously varied factors (architecture depth, regularization, optimizer) remains rare in the literature
Most Fashion-MNIST studies do not report results across multiple fixed random seeds, making it hard to distinguish genuine improvement from seed-dependent variance
The regime in which simple augmentation (flip/rotation/translation) actually helps small CNNs vs. larger or pre-trained models is not well characterized
Short training runs (~5 epochs) may not give augmentation enough time to reduce overfitting, and optimal epoch count for observing augmentation benefit is underexplored
Fashion-MNIST accuracy gains from augmentation appear modest (~1–2%) in short runs, raising the question of whether improvements are practically meaningful given measurement noise
The interaction between augmentation strength (degree of rotation/translation) and dataset difficulty has not been systematically studied on Fashion-MNIST
Reproducibility is inconsistently ensured: many papers omit random seed details, preventing direct comparison of results across studies

gaps.title: Training set size modulates augmentation benefit on Fashion-MNIST

impact.why: Provides concrete guidance on when augmentation is worth applying for practitioners with limited labelled data on Fashion-MNIST-like tasks.

novelty.why: While 'State-of-the-Art Results with the Fashion-MNIST Dataset' examines a small CNN with data augmentation on Fashion-MNIST, none of the prior works systematically vary training set size to measure how augmentation benefit scales and identify a crossover/negligibility point. The proposed study's core contribution—quantifying Δ accuracy vs. log-training-size across subsampled regimes—remains unaddressed.

feasibility.why: Stratified subsampling and 28 short GPU runs are straightforward to implement with torchvision Subset and WeightedRandomSampler.

testability.why: The augmentation benefit vs. training size curve has a clear expected shape and a well-defined crossover point that can be estimated by regression.

gaps.approach: Stratify-subsample the Fashion-MNIST training set at sizes 500, 1,000, 2,500, 5,000, 10,000, 30,000, and 60,000 images using balanced class proportions. Train the fixed small CNN with and without augmentation at each size using seeds 42 and 123 for 5 epochs per run. Plot augmentation benefit (Δ test accuracy) versus log-training-size and fit a simple linear regression on the log scale to identify the crossover point.
gaps.question: How does the test accuracy benefit of basic geometric augmentation scale with training set size for a small CNN on Fashion-MNIST, and at what sample count does the benefit become negligible?
gaps.why_open: (Karadağ et al. 2020) found that 'the contribution of data augmentation is sensitive to the size of the dataset' on CIFAR-10 but this has not been replicated or quantified on Fashion-MNIST. (Kang et al. 2024) shows that MFG Augment 'significantly improves test accuracy when dataset size is small' but for an advanced augmentation method, not basic geometric transforms. (Pham et al. 2018) and (Harun et al. 2024) demonstrate augmentation helps small specialty datasets yet do not characterise the relationship across a systematic range of sample sizes with a fixed architecture and fixed epoch count.
gaps.hypothesis: Augmentation benefit will be largest at small training set sizes (500–5,000 samples) and will decrease monotonically toward negligibility at the full 60,000-sample dataset within 5 epochs, with a crossover point around 10,000–20,000 samples.
gaps.data_needed: Stratified random subsamples of Fashion-MNIST's 60,000-image training split; test set remains the full 10,000 images.

gaps.approach: Train the fixed small CNN with and without augmentation across N=20 independently drawn random seeds for each condition (40 total runs, 5 epochs each). Compute mean, standard deviation, and 95% CI of test accuracy per condition. Perform a Welch t-test and compute Cohen's d. gaps.question: Does the random-seed-induced variance in test accuracy of a small CNN on Fashion-MNIST exceed the typical ~1–2% augmentation benefit, rendering two-seed comparisons statistically unreliable for detecting augmentation effects?

gaps.title: Per-class accuracy differential of basic augmentation Fashion-MNIST

impact.why: Motivates class-adaptive augmentation policies for Fashion-MNIST and provides interpretable diagnostic information for practitioners.

novelty.why: No prior work specifically examines how basic geometric augmentation differentially affects per-class accuracy across morphologically ambiguous vs. distinctive Fashion-MNIST categories; existing class-specific augmentation studies (e.g., 'Class-Adaptive Data Augmentation' and the evolutionary GA approaches) focus on finding optimal per-class augmentation policies rather than measuring the differential benefit of uniform augmentation as a function of class morphological ambiguity.

feasibility.why: Requires only post-hoc analysis of existing model outputs with no additional GPU training, making it the cheapest gap to address.

testability.why: Per-class deltas are clearly computable but statistical power is limited by only 10 classes and 2 seeds, making the permutation test low-powered.

gaps.approach: Extract per-class confusion matrices and per-class F1 scores from the augmented and non-augmented model outputs using saved prediction tensors (from the core study or a short inference pass over the test set). Compute the per-class accuracy delta (aug − no-aug) for all 10 categories across both seeds. Apply a permutation test over the 10 class deltas to assess whether the ranking of per-class benefit is significantly aligned with the known class-difficulty ranking from [3] and [7].
gaps.question: Does basic geometric augmentation differentially benefit or harm classification of morphologically ambiguous versus morphologically distinctive Fashion-MNIST categories?
gaps.why_open: (Yee 2026) and (Ern 2026) document that Fashion-MNIST classes differ markedly in difficulty—Trouser, Bag, and Sandal reach F1 ≥ 0.97 while Shirt and Pullover score ≤ 0.74—but neither paper compares these per-class patterns across augmentation conditions. (Yoo et al. 2023) and (Aguilar et al. 2019) propose class-adaptive augmentation specifically because classes benefit differently from transforms, implying that per-class effects of basic uniform augmentation are an important but unmeasured quantity on Fashion-MNIST. No study reports per-class accuracy delta for basic geometric augmentation on this benchmark.
gaps.hypothesis: Basic augmentation will provide positive accuracy delta for visually ambiguous classes (T-shirt, Shirt, Pullover, Coat) by adding useful pose variation, while providing negligible or slightly negative delta for morphologically distinctive classes (Trouser, Bag, Sandal) that already achieve near-ceiling accuracy without augmentation.
gaps.data_needed: Saved per-sample prediction tensors from augmented and non-augmented trained models; Fashion-MNIST test set class labels.

gaps.title: Ablation of individual augmentation transforms on Fashion-MNIST

impact.why: Actionable for practitioners choosing which transforms to include, but the finding is specific to this narrow architecture-dataset-epoch regime.

novelty.why: None of the prior works specifically isolate and compare the individual contributions of horizontal flip, random translation, and random rotation on Fashion-MNIST with a small CNN, nor do they test for additive vs. interactive effects across these transforms. The closest works (e.g., 'Measuring the Effect of Data Augmentation' and 'Rethinking Efficiency') study augmentation effects but on CIFAR-10/CIFAR-100 with different architectures and without the factorial decomposition proposed here.

feasibility.why: Only 10 GPU runs are required, making this the most computationally lightweight of all proposed investigations.

testability.why: Per-transform accuracy deltas are clearly computable but with only two seeds per condition statistical discrimination of small effects will be limited.

gaps.approach: Train five conditions on the fixed small CNN: (1) no augmentation, (2) flip only, (3) translation only (±10%), (4) rotation only (±10°), and (5) all three combined. Use seeds 42 and 123 for each condition (10 GPU runs, 5 epochs each). Compute pairwise accuracy differences among conditions and fit a linear model with three binary transform indicators to estimate additive contributions and test for interaction terms.
gaps.question: Among horizontal flip, random translation, and random rotation applied to Fashion-MNIST, which individual transform contributes most to test accuracy improvement in a small CNN, and do their effects combine additively?
gaps.why_open: The core study and most prior work including (Greeshma et al. 2019) and (Ern 2026) apply augmentation as a combined bundle without ablating individual transforms. (Hulliyah 2023) uses rotation and shift together on MNIST but does not isolate each transform's contribution or evaluate on Fashion-MNIST. (Hong et al. 2022) finds architectural rotation equivariance outperforms rotation data augmentation on Fashion-MNIST, suggesting rotation augmentation may contribute less than commonly assumed. No study has isolated flip, translation, and rotation contributions under identical small-CNN, Fashion-MNIST, short-training conditions.
gaps.hypothesis: Horizontal flip will contribute the largest individual accuracy gain due to left-right symmetry of most garments, translation will contribute a moderate gain, and rotation will contribute the smallest gain or possibly a small loss at 5 epochs because Fashion-MNIST classes lack 360-degree symmetry and small rotations add little useful variation in the underfitting regime.

impact.why: Directly actionable: practitioners currently choose augmentation parameters by convention rather than data-driven guidance.

novelty.why: The closest work (CNN for Fashion-MNIST with rotation/shift/zoom augmentation) uses augmentation but does not conduct a systematic grid search over rotation × translation magnitudes to map their independent and joint effects on accuracy, nor does it attempt to locate an accuracy-optimal combination or test the inverted-U hypothesis. feasibility.why: 36 GPU runs are at the edge of typical Colab session budgets and require careful job batching and result caching.

testability.why: The heatmap provides a clear outcome but single-seed noise for most grid points may make the identified optimum uncertain.

gaps.approach: Construct a grid of rotation angles (0°, 5°, 10°, 20°, 30°, 45°) crossed with translation magnitudes (0%, 5%, 10%, 20%, 30%), holding horizontal flip constant at on, yielding 30 conditions. Train the fixed small CNN at each grid point with seed 42 for 5 epochs, then re-run the four corner conditions and the apparent optimum with seed 123. Visualise a test-accuracy heatmap over the parameter grid and fit a quadratic surface to locate the optimum.
gaps.question: How do rotation degree and translation magnitude independently affect test accuracy of a small CNN on Fashion-MNIST, and is there an accuracy-optimal parameter combination within the basic augmentation family?
gaps.why_open: The open-problems section explicitly identifies that 'the interaction between augmentation strength (degree of rotation/translation) and dataset difficulty has not been systematically studied on Fashion-MNIST.' (Yoo et al. 2023) derives class-adaptive policies for CIFAR-10 but does not map raw transform magnitude to accuracy for Fashion-MNIST.

plan.background: Data augmentation is widely used to improve CNN generalisation, but the magnitude of its benefit is expected to depend on dataset size: when real data diversity is low, synthetic diversity from augmentation fills a larger gap relative to the total training signal. Prior work on CIFAR-10 found augmentation contribution to be sensitive to dataset size (Karadağ et al. 2020), and a game-theoretic augmentation method showed significant test accuracy improvements specifically in low-data regimes (Kang et al. 2024). Studies on specialty domains such as ultrasound (Snider et al. 2023) and soil images (Maiyanti et al. 2023) corroborate augmentation utility under limited data, yet none systematically quantify the benefit as a continuous function of sample count on Fashion-MNIST. Fashion-MNIST benchmarks consistently report CNNs achieving 88–94% with the full 60,000-image training set (Mukhamediev 2024; Yee 2026; Meshkini et al. 2019; Xhaferra et al. 2022), but no study characterises how basic geometric augmentation benefit evolves across a controlled range from 500 to 60,000 samples on this dataset with a fixed architecture and fixed epoch budget. Establishing this scaling relationship would provide actionable guidance for practitioners deciding whether to apply augmentation at a given data collection budget and would replicate and extend findings from text classification [not in scope here] to image CNNs on a standard benchmark.
plan.hypothesis: Augmentation benefit (Δ test accuracy = acc_aug − acc_noaug) will be largest at small training set sizes (500–5,000 samples), will decrease monotonically as training set size increases on a log scale, and will approach negligibility (Δ < 0.5 percentage points) somewhere between 10,000 and 20,000 samples, consistent with the principle that augmentation provides diminishing returns as real data diversity increases.

open_questions: Does horizontal flip introduce label noise for any Fashion-MNIST class (e.g., sandals or bags may be asymmetric, but most garments are symmetric)? Should flip be excluded from the augmentation set?
Is the 90/10 train/validation split appropriate for N=500 (45 train, 5 val per class)? Would a fixed external validation set be more stable? If so, what size?

Will 5 epochs produce meaningful test accuracy at N=60,000 (expected ~88–90%) or will underfitting make the large-N regime uninformative? Should epoch 5 results be supplemented with a learning-curve extrapolation note?
Does the choice of Adam vs SGD+momentum materially affect the scaling trend? (Out of scope per constraints, but should be acknowledged as a limitation.)
Is log-linear (log base 2) the correct functional form, or would a square-root or power-law fit better? Should AIC/BIC comparison of candidate models be included?
At N=500, are 50 samples per class enough for the CNN to learn any class-discriminative features, or will test accuracy be near chance (10%), making Δ estimates meaningless?
plan.null_hypothesis: Augmentation benefit Δ does not vary systematically with training set size; the expected value of Δ is equal across all seven training set sizes (500, 1,000, 2,500, 5,000, 10,000, 30,000, 60,000).

Total GPU time estimate: 28 runs × mean ~1.5 min/run ≈ 42 GPU minutes; with overhead, budget 2–3 GPU hours. CPU tasks (data prep, analysis, plotting, writing) require < 30 CPU minutes total.

Log-linear regression achieves R² ≥ 0.5, supporting the log-linear scaling model

plan.duration_estimate: 4–6 hours wall-clock for autonomous execution (including Colab startup, sequential GPU training, CPU analysis, and paper compilation)
plan.research_question: How does the test accuracy benefit of basic geometric augmentation (random horizontal flip, ±10% translation, ±10° rotation) scale with training set size from 500 to 60,000 samples for a fixed small CNN on Fashion-MNIST within 5 training epochs, and at what sample count does the benefit become negligible?
plan.validation_strategy: All 28 runs use identical architecture (frozen in `train_fmnist.py`), identical optimizer (Adam, lr=0.001), identical batch size (64), identical epoch count (5), and identical data normalisation statistics (mean=0.2860, std=0.3530 from full training set). Conditions differ only in augmentation policy. Seeds control both subset sampling and model weight initialisation. Validation accuracy is monitored per epoch on a 10%-stratified holdout of each subset (not used for early stopping or model selection — epoch 5 checkpoint always used for test evaluation). The full 10,000-image test set is held out throughout and evaluated only at epoch 5. Robustness checks: (1) class balance of small subsets verified in T1.2; (2) seed concordance on Δ direction reported in T3.4; (3) OLS regression diagnostics (R², residual plot) reported; (4) any negative Δ values explicitly flagged rather than suppressed. Statistical claims are limited to descriptive statistics (mean, range, Spearman ρ) and regression with 95% CI; no p-value-based hypothesis rejection is claimed given only 2 seeds per cell.

outline.title: Abstract
outline.purpose: Summarise the controlled experiment design, the surprising negative primary finding, the directional scaling trend, and the mechanistic interpretation.
key_points: 28 controlled GPU training runs: 7 training set sizes × 2 augmentation conditions × 2 seeds × 5 epochs on NVIDIA L4
Basic geometric augmentation (RandomHorizontalFlip + RandomAffine ±10°/±10%) decreases test accuracy at all tested sizes; mean Δ ranges from −8.06 pp at N=500 to −2.81 pp at N=60,000
Augmentation harm decreases with training set size (Spearman ρ=0.714, log-linear R²=0.613, p=0.037) but crossover to positive benefit is estimated at N*≈6.45 million, far outside the tested range
Result explained by convergence overhead: augmented runs show higher epoch-1 loss in 14/14 configurations; 5 epochs are insufficient for the model to recover
Baseline (no-aug, N=60,000) achieves 91.5% test accuracy, confirming correct CNN calibration

outline.title: Introduction
outline.purpose: Motivate the research question about augmentation scaling with sample count, state the hypothesis, and preview the negative finding.
key_points: Data augmentation widely assumed beneficial for CNN generalisation, especially in low-data regimes
Prior CIFAR-10 work found augmentation benefit is dataset-size sensitive; no systematic Fashion-MNIST study exists across a controlled sample-count range with a fixed architecture and epoch budget
Research question: how does basic geometric augmentation benefit scale with training set size from 500 to 60,000 for a fixed small CNN within 5 epochs?
Main finding: augmentation consistently hurts under 5-epoch budget; harm decreases with N but no crossover observed within tested regime
Contribution: first systematic quantification of augmentation benefit scaling on Fashion-MNIST; cautionary evidence that short training runs can invert augmentation's expected benefit

outline.title: Related Work
outline.purpose: Situate the study within CNN Fashion-MNIST benchmarks, augmentation effect literature, and low-data regime studies.
key_points: Small CNN benchmarks on Fashion-MNIST: 88–94% accuracy with full training set; our no-aug baseline (91.5%) is consistent with this range
Data augmentation generally reported to improve CNN generalisation but magnitude varies by training budget and architecture depth
Karadağ et al. (2020) showed CIFAR-10 augmentation benefit is dataset-size sensitive — motivating replication and extension to Fashion-MNIST
Kang et al. (2024) showed advanced augmentation benefits small datasets specifically; our work examines basic transforms and a stricter epoch budget
Pham et al. (2018) and Harun et al. (2024) found augmentation helpful for speciality small-data domains but used much longer training runs (>>5 epochs)
No prior work quantifies the augmentation benefit as a continuous function of training set size on Fashion-MNIST under a fixed architecture and epoch count

outline.title: Methods
outline.purpose: Describe the experimental design, architecture, augmentation policy, training protocol, and analysis pipeline in full reproducible detail.
key_points: Small CNN: two dual-conv blocks (Conv 1→32→32 → MaxPool → Dropout(0.25), Conv 32→64→64 → MaxPool → Dropout(0.25)) + FC head (3136→256→ReLU→Dropout(0.5)→10) with BatchNorm; 871,018 parameters
Augmentation condition 'aug': RandomHorizontalFlip(p=0.5) + RandomAffine(degrees=10, translate=(0.1,0.1)); test-time transform always no-augmentation
Training: Adam (lr=0.001), batch size 64, 5 epochs, CrossEntropyLoss, no LR scheduler; identical across all conditions

Data: Fashion-MNIST 60,000 train / 10,000 test; 7 stratified class-balanced subsets (N=500, 1000, 2500, 5000, 10000, 30000, 60000) with 90/10 train/val split per subset; seeds 42 and 123 for both subset sampling and weight initialisation
28 total runs on NVIDIA L4, PyTorch 2.11.0+cu130; per-epoch train loss, val accuracy, and epoch-5 test accuracy recorded

Analysis: mean Δ = acc_aug − acc_noaug per size; OLS log-linear regression Δ = a + b·log₂(N); bootstrap N* estimation (5,000 iterations, seed=42); Spearman ρ for monotonicity; all analysis is descriptive given n=2 seeds

outline.title: Results
outline.purpose: Report all empirical findings: per-size Δ values, training curves, regression statistics, monotonicity diagnostics, and baseline calibration.
key_points: Perfect seed concordance: 7/7 sizes, both seeds produce negative Δ (concordance fraction 1.00)
Log-linear regression: Δ = −12.00 + 0.530·log₂(N), R²=0.613, p=0.037; slope 95% CI [0.046, 1.015]; augmentation harm decreases with log N
Crossover N*=6.45 million (bootstrap 95% CI [40,325; ~1 billion]) — extrapolated far above tested range; N* note flags extrapolation
Spearman ρ=0.714 (p=0.071): positive monotone trend not reaching α=0.05 significance with n=7; non-monotone dip at N=5,000–10,000
Augmented runs show higher epoch-1 loss in 14/14 configurations: convergence overhead confirmed as mechanistic explanation
Baseline no-aug accuracy at N=60,000: seed 42=91.40%, seed 123=91.57%, mean 91.48% — within 88–92% expected range

outline.title: Discussion
outline.purpose: Interpret the negative finding mechanistically, compare with prior expectations and literature, and contextualise the crossover uncertainty.
key_points: Universal negative Δ is best explained by augmentation's convergence overhead: harder per-step examples (14/14 higher epoch-1 loss) require more epochs to overcome than the 5-epoch budget allows
This is effectively a form of data hardening that reduces per-step gradient informativeness; the CNN cannot recover its baseline performance within 5 epochs under this harder signal

The positive OLS slope and Spearman ρ suggest that at larger N the model trains faster in absolute terms and partially recovers: consistent with more gradient steps (larger batches cover more data per epoch) providing more informative parameter updates even under augmentation

Non-monotone dip at N=5,000–10,000 may reflect an inflection where overfitting in the no-augmentation condition accelerates relative to the augmented model's slower convergence, temporarily widening the gap before the augmented model catches up at larger N
The N*=6.45 million estimate should be treated as an illustration of the regression framework only; the bootstrap CI spanning [40K; 1B] reflects genuine extrapolation uncertainty

Prior studies finding augmentation beneficial (Pham et al. 2018 on skin lesions, Snider et al. 2023 on ultrasound) used training runs of 50–200+ epochs; the apparent contradiction is fully explained by epoch budget differences

Practical implication: practitioners should not apply basic geometric augmentation in short-run training pipelines (≤5 epochs) without verifying that training time is sufficient for convergence recovery

outline.title: Limitations
outline.purpose: Honestly enumerate the study's constraints and their impact on generalisability.
key_points: Two seeds per cell prevent formal significance testing; Spearman ρ and OLS regression are descriptive only; p=0.071 does not reach α=0.05
5-epoch budget is a single highly constrained protocol; results are specific to this under-trained regime and not generalisable to longer training runs
Non-monotone mid-range trend (N=5,000–10,000 dip) reduces confidence in the log-linear model as a complete description
N* bootstrap CI spans four orders of magnitude; point estimate of 6.45 million has negligible predictive utility
Single architecture and single basic augmentation policy; results may not hold for larger models, different regularisation configurations, or more sophisticated augmentation
Fashion-MNIST-specific findings; extrapolation to CIFAR-10 or other benchmarks requires separate experiments

outline.title: Conclusion
outline.purpose: Summarise the main finding and its practical implication concisely.
key_points: Basic geometric augmentation consistently hurts a small CNN on Fashion-MNIST under a 5-epoch training budget at all sample sizes from 500 to 60,000
Augmentation harm decreases as training set size grows (R²=0.613) but no crossover to positive benefit is observed within the tested regime; the estimated N*≈6.45M is unreliably extrapolated
The result is explained by insufficient training time to overcome augmentation's convergence overhead, not by inherent augmentation inferiority
Practitioners should ensure sufficient training epochs before applying augmentation; the benefit of augmentation is epoch-budget-dependent, not just dataset-size-dependent
Future work should vary epoch budget systematically to identify the minimum epoch count at which basic augmentation becomes beneficial at each training set size

outline.title: Abstract
outline.purpose: Summarise the experimental design, the unexpected key finding that augmentation uniformly hurts within 5 epochs, the log-linear scaling trend, and the mechanistic explanation.
key_points: Studied how basic geometric augmentation benefit scales with training set size (500–60,000) for a fixed small CNN on Fashion-MNIST in exactly 5 epochs
Augmentation decreased test accuracy by 2.8–8.1 pp at all 7 training sizes; no positive benefit observed at any size
The harm decreases monotonically with log₂(N): fitted Δ = −12.0 + 0.53·log₂N, R²=0.613, p=0.037
Crossover N* ≈ 6.45M (bootstrap 95% CI [40,325–1×10⁹]) is extrapolated far beyond the tested maximum of 60,000
Mechanistic explanation: augmented runs show higher epoch-1 training loss in 14/14 configurations, confirming convergence slowdown as the cause

outline.title: Introduction
outline.purpose: Motivate the study by framing the open question of how augmentation benefit scales with training set size on Fashion-MNIST, and situate it in the context of prior work on CIFAR-10 and specialty domains.
key_points: Data augmentation is widely adopted as a regulariser for CNNs but its benefit depends on training set size
Karadağ et al. (2020) found augmentation contribution sensitive to dataset size on CIFAR-10 but this has not been replicated on Fashion-MNIST with a controlled, fixed-epoch protocol

Kang et al. (2024) demonstrated augmentation benefits with MFG Augment, a Mean-Field Game path-interpolation method that synthesises continuous image distribution transitions, showing significant improvements in low-data regimes; the effect of basic geometric transforms in the same regime is unstudied
Prior work on specialty domains (medical imaging, soil classification) demonstrates augmentation utility under limited data but does not characterise the continuous scaling relationship
This study provides the first controlled quantification of basic geometric augmentation benefit scaling from 500 to 60,000 samples on Fashion-MNIST with fixed architecture and epoch count

outline.title: Related Work
outline.purpose: Review CNN benchmarking on Fashion-MNIST, the general effect of augmentation, dataset-size interactions, and advanced augmentation strategies.
key_points: Fashion-MNIST CNN baselines: small two-block CNNs achieve 88–91% test accuracy (Yee 2026; Meshkini et al. 2019; Mukhamediev 2024), providing the reference range for our no-augmentation baseline at N=60,000
Augmentation generally improves generalisation especially in low-data regimes (Pham et al. 2018; Harun et al. 2024; Snider et al. 2023; Maiyanti et al. 2023), typically over longer training runs
Karadağ et al. (2020) quantified augmentation sensitivity to dataset size on CIFAR-10 using VAEs; our study replicates and extends this design to Fashion-MNIST with basic geometric transforms

Kumar et al. (2025) proposed three novel augmentation techniques — pairwise channel transfer, object occlusion, and masking — that improve CNN performance on small datasets, demonstrating that carefully designed augmentation strategies can meaningfully reduce overfitting in limited-data regimes

Kang et al. (2024) demonstrated augmentation benefits with MFG Augment, a Mean-Field Game path-interpolation method that synthesises continuous image distribution transitions, which is substantially more sophisticated than the simple geometric transforms used here

Advanced policies (WeMix, LMix) and class-conditional augmentation outperform basic transforms but at higher computational cost; circular shift augmentation (Zhang et al. 2020) specifically targets invariance to spatial shifts
The 5-epoch training regime is an acknowledged constraint relative to the long-run evaluations typical in prior work

outline.title: Methods
outline.purpose: Describe the experimental design, CNN architecture, training protocol, stratified subsampling, and statistical analysis pipeline in sufficient detail for reproduction.
key_points: Architecture: SmallCNN with two double-conv blocks (Conv(1→32→32)+BN+ReLU+MaxPool+Dropout(0.25); Conv(32→64→64)+BN+ReLU+MaxPool+Dropout(0.25)) followed by FC(3136→256→10) with Dropout(0.5); 871,018 parameters; identical across all conditions
Training: Adam lr=0.001, batch_size=64, 5 epochs, CrossEntropyLoss; no LR scheduler; identical hyperparameters across conditions
Augmentation (aug): RandomHorizontalFlip(p=0.5) + RandomAffine(degrees=10, translate=(0.1,0.1)); no augmentation at test time in either condition

Subset sampling: seven stratified sizes (500, 1000, 2500, 5000, 10000, 30000, 60000) with exactly N//10 per class; 90/10 train/val StratifiedShuffleSplit; seeds 42 and 123; indices persisted in data/subset_indices.npz and class balance verified
Evaluation: final test accuracy on full 10,000-image test set at epoch 5 only; validation accuracy monitored per epoch but not used for model selection or early stopping
Analysis: mean Δ per size; OLS log-linear regression Δ = a + b·log₂(N) over 7 size levels; bootstrap N* CI (5,000 iterations); Spearman ρ for monotonicity; all descriptive only given n=2 seeds
Hardware: NVIDIA L4 GPU, CUDA 13.0, PyTorch 2.11.0+cu130, Python 3.13.15

outline.title: Results
outline.purpose: Present all empirical findings: per-size test accuracies, Δ values by seed and mean, regression fit, monotonicity diagnostics, convergence analysis, and baseline calibration check.
key_points: No-augmentation baseline rises monotonically from 73.4% (N=500) to 91.5% (N=60,000), confirming the CNN is well-calibrated against published benchmarks (88–92% range for similar small CNNs)
Perfect seed concordance: both seeds independently produce negative Δ at all 7 sizes (7/7), ruling out seed artefact
OLS log-linear regression: Δ = −12.0 + 0.530·log₂N, R²=0.613, p=0.037; slope 95% CI [0.046, 1.015]
Spearman ρ=+0.714 (p=0.071): strong positive rank correlation between N and Δ, indicating the harm becomes less severe at larger training sizes
Crossover N*=6,448,676 (bootstrap 95% CI [40,325–1×10⁹]); extrapolated far above the tested maximum; augmentation does not break even within the studied regime
In all 14 (seed×size) pairs, epoch-1 training loss is higher under augmentation (14/14), confirming augmentation imposes a convergence cost that cannot be recovered in 5 epochs

outline.title: Discussion
outline.purpose: Interpret the convergence-slowdown finding, relate to prior literature, discuss the log-linear scaling trend, and draw practical implications.
key_points: The universal negative Δ is explained by the epoch-budget effect: augmented samples are harder per step, requiring more epochs to recover the convergence deficit; 5 epochs is insufficient at all tested sizes

The log-linear scaling trend (less harm at larger N) is consistent with the theoretical expectation that larger real-data diversity reduces the relative disadvantage imposed by augmentation's added difficulty

This finding does not contradict prior literature (Pham et al. 2018; Harun et al. 2024; Maiyanti et al. 2023), which typically uses much longer training; it contextualises their results as epoch-budget-dependent

Karadağ et al. (2020)'s observation of augmentation sensitivity to dataset size on CIFAR-10 is confirmed directionally: harm does decrease with N; the sign reversal reveals the short-epoch regime as a distinct regime

MFG Augment (Kang et al. 2024), which synthesises continuous paths between image distributions via Mean-Field Game theory, likely avoids the convergence penalty because its interpolated samples are smoother and more natural than hard geometric transforms applied here
Practitioners should treat epoch budget as a critical factor when applying basic geometric augmentation: in short-training regimes the convergence cost may dominate any regularisation benefit
The wide N* CI ([40,325–1×10⁹]) shows that reliably estimating the crossover point would require more seeds, intermediate sizes, and varied epoch counts beyond the scope of this study

outline.title: Limitations
outline.purpose: Honestly enumerate the constraints on statistical and external validity of this study.
key_points: Only two seeds per cell; no formal significance testing claimed; all comparisons are descriptive
5-epoch budget is unusually short; results are specific to this low-epoch regime
Single augmentation policy tested; stronger or class-adaptive policies may behave differently
Crossover N* is an unreliable extrapolation given the extremely wide bootstrap CI
Results specific to Fashion-MNIST and the fixed architecture; generalisation to other datasets or deeper models is untested
Non-monotone raw Δ pattern (most negative at N=5,000–10,000) suggests a more complex underlying relationship than log-linear; R²=0.613 leaves 39% of variance unexplained

outline.title: Conclusion
outline.purpose: Summarise the main takeaway and its practical implication for practitioners applying augmentation to Fashion-MNIST-like tasks.
key_points: Within a 5-epoch budget, basic geometric augmentation (flip, rotation, translation) consistently decreased test accuracy at all training sizes from 500 to 60,000 on Fashion-MNIST
The harm follows a log-linear scaling with training set size: Δ = −12.0 + 0.53·log₂N (R²=0.613), diminishing but not disappearing across the studied range
Augmentation would only be expected to break even at N*≈6.45M samples — an extrapolation underscoring the epoch-budget dependency of augmentation benefit

The principal practical recommendation is that epoch budget must be considered when applying basic augmentation: in short-training regimes augmentation's convergence cost can outweigh its regularisation benefit
Future work should vary epoch count to identify the training-length threshold above which basic augmentation becomes beneficial for Fashion-MNIST-scale tasks

However, the sign of Δ is reversed from predictions: all seven mean Δ values are negative (ranging from −8.1 pp at N=500 to −2.8 pp at N=60,000), meaning augmentation consistently hurts rather than helps within 5 epochs. The crossover N*≈6.45M is extrapolated far beyond the tested maximum of 60,000 (bootstrap 95% CI: [40,325–1×10⁹]), contradicting the predicted 10,000–20,000 crossover. The mechanistic cause is confirmed: augmented runs produce higher epoch-1 training loss in all 14 (seed×size) configurations, consistent with augmentation slowing convergence faster than the 5-epoch budget allows recovery.

outline.title: Abstract
outline.purpose: Summarise the research question, method, and key finding (augmentation hurts at all sizes under 5 epochs; penalty decreases log-linearly with N) in ~150 words.
key_points: Research question: how does augmentation benefit scale with training set size for a small CNN on Fashion-MNIST within 5 epochs?
28 runs: 7 sizes × 2 conditions × 2 seeds on NVIDIA L4 GPU
Main finding: Δ negative at all sizes (−8.1 pp at N=500 to −2.8 pp at N=60,000)
Log-linear model R²=0.613, p=0.037; crossover N* extrapolated at ~6.45M
Conclusion: 5-epoch budget insufficient for basic augmentation to help; augmentation becomes progressively less harmful as N grows

outline.title: Introduction
outline.purpose: Motivate the study by establishing that augmentation sensitivity to dataset size is an important but under-characterised phenomenon on Fashion-MNIST, and state the research question and contributions.
key_points: Fashion-MNIST is a standard benchmark with published small-CNN baselines in the 88–92% range
Data augmentation is widely applied but its benefit is expected to depend on dataset size

Karadağ et al. (2020) found augmentation contribution sensitive to dataset size on CIFAR-10; kang2024game showed MFG Augment significantly improves accuracy in low-data regimes (do not attribute Mixup/CutOut to this work)
Gap: no controlled study on Fashion-MNIST systematically varies N from 500 to 60,000 with fixed architecture, fixed epoch count, and fixed seeds
Contribution: 28 GPU-trained experiments producing Δ vs N curve, log-linear regression, crossover estimation, and reproducible codebase

outline.title: Related Work
outline.purpose: Survey prior work on (1) CNN benchmarks on Fashion-MNIST establishing baselines, (2) augmentation sensitivity to dataset size, and (3) augmentation in low-data regimes, highlighting the gap this study fills.
key_points: CNN baselines on Fashion-MNIST: small two-block CNNs typically achieve 88–90% with full training set (mukhamediev2024state, yee2026based, meshkini2019analysis, xhaferra2022classification)
Augmentation sensitivity to dataset size: karada2020empirical found augmentation contribution sensitive to dataset size on CIFAR-10; this has not been replicated on Fashion-MNIST

Low-data augmentation: pham2018deep (skin lesion), harun2024dysgraphia, snider2023using (ultrasound), maiyanti2023rotation (soil) all show augmentation helps small specialty datasets but do not characterise the scaling relationship

Novel augmentation strategies: kang2024game demonstrated benefits with MFG Augment (Mean-Field Game path-interpolation, not Mixup/CutOut); kumar2025enhancing proposed three novel techniques (pairwise channel transfer, object occlusion, masking) improving CNN performance on small datasets
Epoch budget effects on augmentation: augmentation typically requires more epochs to converge; this confound is rarely controlled in the literature

outline.title: Methods
outline.purpose: Describe the experimental design: architecture, training configuration, data subsampling, evaluation, and statistical analysis, with enough detail for full reproducibility.
key_points: Architecture: SmallCNN with two conv blocks (Conv→BN→ReLU×2→MaxPool→Dropout(0.25)), FC(3136,256)→Dropout(0.5)→FC(10); identical across all 28 runs
Training: Adam lr=0.001, batch size=64, 5 epochs, CrossEntropyLoss, no scheduler; CUDA on NVIDIA L4
Data: Fashion-MNIST; 7 training sizes (500,1000,2500,5000,10000,30000,60000) stratified subsampled with exactly N/10 per class; 90/10 train/val split via StratifiedShuffleSplit; seeds 42 and 123
Augmentation: RandomHorizontalFlip(p=0.5)+RandomAffine(degrees=10,translate=(0.1,0.1)) vs no augmentation; normalization mean=0.2860,std=0.3530 identical for both conditions
Evaluation: full 10,000-image test set evaluated only at epoch 5; augmentation not applied at test time
Analysis: Δ = acc_aug − acc_noaug per (size,seed); mean and range across seeds; OLS log-linear regression Δ = a + b·log₂(N); Spearman ρ; bootstrap N* (5000 iterations); concordance check

outline.title: Results
outline.purpose: Report all empirical findings: per-size Δ values, training curves, regression model, crossover estimation, and baseline calibration.
key_points: Augmentation hurts at all 7 sizes: Δ ranges from −8.1 pp (N=500, mean of −6.91 and −9.20) to −2.8 pp (N=60,000, mean of −2.88 and −2.73)
Non-monotone local behaviour: Δ at N=5,000 (−6.6 pp) is more negative than at N=2,500 (−4.8 pp), suggesting size-specific dynamics
Perfect seed concordance: both seeds agree on negative sign at all 7 sizes (7/7)
Log-linear OLS: Δ = −12.00 + 0.530·log₂(N), R²=0.613, p=0.037; moderate fit with monotone positive slope
Spearman ρ=+0.714 (p=0.071): strong positive rank correlation — Δ increases toward zero as N increases
Crossover N*≈6.45M (bootstrap 95% CI [40,325 – 1×10⁹]): extrapolated far outside tested range, uninformative as a practical threshold
Baseline: no-aug accuracy at N=60,000 is 91.48% mean (91.40% and 91.57% per seed), within 88–92% expected range
Epoch-1 loss: augmented runs show higher training loss than no-aug in all 14 configurations (14/14)

outline.title: Discussion
outline.purpose: Interpret the unexpected result (augmentation hurts under 5 epochs), connect to the epoch-budget mechanism, compare to prior work expectations, and discuss implications.
key_points: The finding that augmentation consistently hurts within 5 epochs is mechanistically explained by augmentation increasing per-step difficulty (higher epoch-1 loss at all sizes), which the model cannot recover from in 5 epochs
This is consistent with known augmentation behaviour: transforms introduce variance that requires more gradient updates to smooth out, requiring longer training horizons

The positive OLS slope (b=+0.530) indicates augmentation becomes progressively less harmful as N increases, likely because larger datasets already provide more diversity per batch, reducing the fractional overhead of augmented variance

Comparison to karada2020empirical (CIFAR-10): the finding that augmentation contribution is sensitive to dataset size is replicated on Fashion-MNIST, but the direction is opposite when training epochs are insufficient

Comparison to kang2024game (MFG Augment): that method, which synthesises continuous image distribution transitions rather than simple geometric transforms, showed benefit in low-data regimes; basic transforms studied here are insufficient
The wide bootstrap CI on N* ([40,325 – 1×10⁹]) means the crossover point is practically unknowable from these data; practitioners should not use 5-epoch runs to assess augmentation utility
Practical guidance: for Fashion-MNIST-like tasks with tight epoch budgets, basic geometric augmentation may not help and could hurt; longer training runs should be used to assess augmentation benefit

outline.title: Limitations
outline.purpose: Enumerate the methodological constraints that bound the generalisability of the findings.
key_points: Only two seeds per cell: descriptive statistics only, no formal significance testing
5-epoch budget is the root cause of negative Δ and limits generalisability to longer training
Non-monotone local Δ trend reduces confidence in the log-linear model
N* bootstrap CI too wide for actionable guidance
Single dataset (Fashion-MNIST), single architecture, single augmentation policy
No learning-rate scheduler; augmented runs may benefit more from LR decay

outline.title: Conclusion
outline.purpose: Summarise the key finding, its significance, and directions for future work in 1–2 paragraphs.
key_points: Within a 5-epoch budget, basic geometric augmentation (flip, rotation, translation) consistently reduces test accuracy for a small CNN on Fashion-MNIST at all training set sizes from 500 to 60,000
The augmentation penalty decreases as training set size grows on a log scale (OLS R²=0.613), but a breakeven point is not achieved within the tested range

The primary implication is that practitioners using tight epoch budgets should validate augmentation on a held-out set before deployment; 5 epochs is insufficient for the studied transforms to be beneficial
Future work: extend to longer training runs (50+ epochs) to observe the positive augmentation regime; test across more seeds; compare to more sophisticated augmentation methods such as MFG Augment

The experiments show Δ is negative at every tested size: −8.1 pp at N=500 and −2.8 pp at N=60,000 (analysis/delta_by_size.csv). The crossover N* where Δ=0 is estimated at ~6.45 million samples, far outside the tested range (analysis/regression_results.json, N_star=6,448,676, bootstrap 95% CI [40,325 – 1×10⁹], flagged extrapolated_above_range). These findings reflect augmentation becoming progressively less harmful at larger N, but the fundamental claim—that augmentation provides positive benefit—is falsified across all conditions within a 5-epoch budget. The root cause is that augmented runs consistently incur higher epoch-1 training loss (14/14 comparisons), and 5 epochs are insufficient for the model to recover the additional variance introduced by the transforms.

Use language like 'consistent with', 'suggestive of', 'descriptive evidence'. (2) The log-linear model (R²=0.613) is moderate, not conclusive. (3) The crossover N*≈6.45M is an extrapolation with a bootstrap CI spanning three orders of magnitude; describe it as practically unknowable from these data. (4) Do not describe the Spearman ρ=+0.714 as confirming the hypothesis direction — the hypothesis predicted positive Δ decreasing toward zero, not negative Δ increasing toward zero. outline.title: Abstract
outline.purpose: Summarise the experimental design, the unexpected key finding (augmentation uniformly harmful within 5 epochs), the log-linear trend, and the practical implication.
key_points: Fashion-MNIST, small CNN, 7 training sizes (500–60,000), 2 seeds, 5 epochs on NVIDIA L4 GPU
Augmentation (flip, ±10° rotation, ±10% translation) reduced test accuracy at all sizes; mean Δ from −8.06 pp (N=500) to −2.81 pp (N=60,000)
Log-linear OLS: Δ = −12.00 + 0.531·log₂(N), R² = 0.613, p = 0.037; augmentation becomes less costly at larger N but never breaks even
Crossover N* ≈ 6.45M, far outside tested range; 5 epochs insufficient for augmented convergence
Limitation: 2 seeds only; results are exploratory; the epoch budget is the primary confound

outline.title: Introduction
outline.purpose: Motivate the study as a controlled characterisation of how augmentation benefit scales with N, identify the gap in prior work on Fashion-MNIST, and state the hypothesis.
key_points: Augmentation is widely used but its benefit is not uniform across data regimes
Prior work on CIFAR-10 found augmentation contribution sensitive to dataset size (Karadağ et al. 2020); systematic characterisation on Fashion-MNIST is absent
Kang et al. (2024) showed MFG Augment significantly improves accuracy in low-data regimes, but for a sophisticated game-theoretic method, not basic geometric transforms
Pham et al. (2018) and Harun et al. (2024) demonstrate augmentation helps specialty small datasets but do not characterise the N-scaling relationship with a fixed architecture
This study: 7 training sizes, fixed architecture, fixed 5-epoch budget, 2 seeds, basic geometric transforms only
Hypothesis stated: benefit largest at small N, decreasing log-linearly, crossover ~10K–20K

outline.title: Related Work
outline.purpose: Situate the study within CNN benchmarking on Fashion-MNIST and augmentation literature, with accurate citations.
key_points: Fashion-MNIST simple CNNs achieve 88–94% with full training data (Meshkini et al. 2019; Mukhamediev 2024; Yee 2026)
Basic augmentation (flips, rotations, circular shifts) generally reduces overfitting in limited-data regimes (Poojary et al. 2021; Zhang et al. 2020; Shawky et al. 2020)

\citet{kang2024game} demonstrated augmentation benefits with MFG Augment, a Mean-Field Game path-interpolation method that synthesises continuous image distribution transitions, which is substantially more sophisticated than the simple geometric transforms used here — do NOT attribute Mixup or CutOut to this work

\citet{kumar2025enhancing} proposed three novel augmentation techniques — pairwise channel transfer, object occlusion, and masking — that improve CNN performance on small datasets, demonstrating that carefully designed augmentation strategies can meaningfully reduce overfitting in limited-data regimes — do NOT characterise as a survey or attribute the 'training budget' conclusion
Snider et al. (2023) and Maiyanti et al. (2023) show augmentation utility in specialty small datasets; no prior work systematically quantifies Δ as a function of N on Fashion-MNIST
Advanced methods (WeMix, LMix, class-conditional policies) outperform naive augmentation by correcting distribution shift (Xu et al. 2020; Yan et al. 2022; Yoo et al. 2023)

outline.title: Methods
outline.purpose: Describe the experimental design, architecture, training protocol, augmentation policy, and statistical analysis.
key_points: Dataset: Fashion-MNIST 60,000 train / 10,000 test; stratified subsets at N = 500, 1,000, 2,500, 5,000, 10,000, 30,000, 60,000 (exactly N/10 per class, verified balanced)
Architecture: SmallCNN — two blocks of Conv→BN→ReLU→Conv→BN→ReLU→MaxPool(2)→Dropout(0.25) with filters 32/32 and 64/64; head FC(3136→256)→ReLU→Dropout(0.5)→FC(256→10)
Optimizer: Adam, lr=0.001, batch=64; 5 epochs; no LR scheduler; identical across all conditions
Augmentation (aug): RandomHorizontalFlip(p=0.5), RandomAffine(degrees=10, translate=(0.1,0.1)); no-aug: ToTensor+Normalize only
Seeds 42 and 123 control both subset sampling and weight initialisation; 28 total runs (7 sizes × 2 conditions × 2 seeds)
Evaluation: full 10,000-image test set at epoch 5 only; 90/10 stratified train/val split per subset
Statistics: Δ = acc_aug − acc_noaug per (size, seed); OLS log-linear regression on log₂(N); Spearman ρ; bootstrap N* CI (5,000 iterations, seed=42); no formal hypothesis rejection given n=2 seeds
Hardware: NVIDIA L4 GPU, CUDA 13.0, PyTorch 2.11.0+cu130

outline.title: Results
outline.purpose: Report all 28 test accuracies, augmentation benefit Δ at each size, regression results, and diagnostic statistics with supporting figures and table.
key_points: No-aug baseline at N=60,000: seed 42 = 91.40%, seed 123 = 91.57% (mean 91.48%), confirming well-calibrated model
Spearman ρ = 0.714, p = 0.071 (marginal at α=0.10; limited power with n=7)
N* ≈ 6.45M, bootstrap 95% CI [40,325 – 1B], flagged extrapolated_above_range
Seed concordance 7/7; epoch-1 aug loss > noaug loss in 14/14 configurations
Non-monotone middle: N=5,000–10,000 show larger deficit than N=1,000

outline.title: Discussion
outline.purpose: Interpret the unexpected negative-Δ finding, explain the convergence bottleneck mechanism, relate to prior literature, and discuss practical implications.
key_points: Central finding coherent mechanistically: augmentation raises per-step difficulty, confirmed by 14/14 epoch-1 loss comparisons; 5 epochs insufficient for recovery
Log-linear trend consistent with principle that real data diversity reduces marginal cost of augmented diversity; with more data the model converges faster even under harder transforms
Prior work finding augmentation beneficial (Karadağ et al. 2020 on CIFAR-10; Pham et al. 2018 on skin lesions) involved longer training or more careful augmentation design
MFG Augment (Kang et al. 2024) may avoid the convergence-delay cost by generating informative interpolated samples rather than simply adding geometric noise
Non-monotone middle range may reflect batch-size-to-dataset-size ratio effects or stochastic variability with 2 seeds
Practical message: do not apply basic augmentation uncritically in time-constrained training; ensure sufficient epochs or use adaptive augmentation

outline.title: Limitations
outline.purpose: State scope boundaries and caveats clearly.
key_points: Two seeds only; results are exploratory; no formal significance testing
5-epoch budget is primary confound; results may reverse with more epochs
Single architecture and dataset; generalisation not claimed
N* is highly extrapolated; CI spans three orders of magnitude
Augmentation strength is a fixed choice; optimal policy may vary with N
Architecture has BatchNorm and Dropout which may reduce marginal augmentation benefit

outline.title: Conclusion
outline.purpose: Summarise the key empirical contribution and actionable takeaway for practitioners.
key_points: Under a strict 5-epoch budget, basic geometric augmentation consistently reduced Fashion-MNIST test accuracy for a small CNN across N=500 to N=60,000
The deficit diminished log-linearly with N (R²=0.613) but augmentation did not break even within the tested range
Practitioners: basic augmentation should not be applied uncritically in short training regimes; sufficient epoch budget for convergence is required
Future work: characterise epoch-count threshold for break-even; test more sophisticated methods such as MFG Augment that may avoid convergence delay

scaffold.verdict_explanation: The hypothesis predicted positive augmentation benefit (Δ = acc_aug − acc_noaug) largest at small N (500–5,000 samples), monotonically decreasing, with a crossover around 10,000–20,000. The root cause, confirmed in 14/14 seed × size configurations, is that augmented runs show higher epoch-1 training loss, indicating augmentation slows convergence below what 5 epochs can recover.
